alt: Three tiers. Social structures such as families and the education system work on people through social processes such as socialisation and labelling, which create social issues such as divorce, underachievement, crime and poverty. Below, a line from structure to agency: functionalist and Marxist accounts stress structure; interactionist accounts stress meanings and labels.
caption: Structures act on people through processes, and the results become debated issues.

after: ## Comparing and contrasting theories in context
alt: Two overlapping ovals. Functionalism and Marxism both explain behaviour by social structure; Marxism and feminism are both conflict theories that see institutions serving a powerful group, so Marxism sits in the overlap. Interactionism stands apart, starting from small-scale interaction.
caption: Find the similarity first: Marxism shares structure with functionalism and conflict with feminism.

after: ## Comparing and contrasting theories in context
alt: One question in the centre, who benefits from the family, with three answers: Parsons says members and society; Zaretsky says capitalism, through unpaid domestic labour and consumption; Delphy and Leonard say men, who appropriate women’s work. A note judges which fits a dual-earner couple.
caption: Put two theories on the same question, then judge which fits the evidence better.

alt: Five numbered questions: who and when, which perspective, the main claim, the evidence and the limits. Below, signal words: value consensus and functions for functionalists, capitalism and ruling class for Marxists, patriarchy and men benefit for feminists, label and meanings for interactionists.
caption: Ask five questions of every extract; signal words reveal the perspective.

after: ## Methods and methodological issues in each topic
alt: Three columns. Divorce statistics count legal divorces but miss separations and empty shell marriages. Crime statistics count recorded crime but miss the dark figure. Poverty figures depend on the definition: just over 6%, a little over 9% or more than 22% for the same society in 1968–69.
caption: Official statistics are useful, but each topic has gaps the numbers do not show.

after: ## Methods and methodological issues in each topic
alt: Six named studies sorted by approach. Quantitative: Halsey, Heath and Ridge (over 8,000 males), Townsend (over 2,000 households) and Willmott and Young (nearly 2,000 people). Qualitative: Ball (one school), Willis (one Midlands school) and Carlen (39 women). Each shows its method and one limitation.
caption: Large samples give patterns; small, deep studies give meanings.

after: ## Contemporary social issues: challenging everyday understandings
alt: Four everyday beliefs, each with a sociological challenge: crime statistics reflect labelling (Becker); women are controlled more closely (Heidensohn); class shapes school success (Halsey, Bowles and Gintis); the private family is an illusion (Zaretsky). Below, Murray and Townsend on poverty.
caption: Everyday views blame nature or choice; sociology looks for the structures behind them.

alt: Four concepts that run across the course: labelling links education and crime (Ball, Becker); social control links families and crime (Heidensohn); class links education, crime and stratification (Halsey, Cohen, Carlen); patriarchy links families and stratification (Delphy and Leonard, Walby).
caption: The same concepts appear in several topics; linking them strengthens an argument.
